title: Do This If You Want Another Year of Windows 10 Security Updates
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Michal Krakowiak/Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft is offering another year of Windows 10 security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027.
                                            If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action.
                                            Other users can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you are still holding on to Windows 10, there's good news: Microsoft is offering another year of security updates, pushing the Windows 11 upgrade deadline back to Oct. 12, 2027. Microsoft officially ended support for the older OS last year but allowed users to join the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program in order to maintain protection against viruses and hackers. ESU coverage was supposed to expire on Oct. 13, 2026, but the company is allowing enrolled Windows 10 users to receive monthly patches for another year—and it's not too late to sign up if you haven't already.  You can stay on Windows 10 through Oct. 2027If you're already in Microsoft's ESU program, your coverage will automatically continue through Oct. 12, 2027 without any additional action on your part. If you haven't, though, you can enroll in ESU at any time until the program ends next year. To be eligible, your device must be running Windows 10 version 22H2 Home, Professional, Pro Education, or Workstations editions and have the latest Windows update installed. You must also be signed into a Microsoft account with administrator status. 
Windows users were originally able to purchase ESU coverage for $30, and Microsoft later added the option to either redeem 1,000 Microsoft Rewards points or opt into Windows Backup to get protection for free. To check your coverage or sign up, go to Settings > Update & Security > Windows Update and look for an ESU enrollment link (visible if your device is eligible). Follow the prompts to sign into your Microsoft account and choose your enrollment option. If you've already purchased an ESU license, you can apply it to up to 10 devices running Windows 10 as long as they are linked to your Microsoft account. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The ESU program does not include any new features or non-security updates, but if you want to stay on Windows 10, it's highly recommended that you enroll in the program. Microsoft has started pushing hundreds of critical security fixes each month—a handful of which have been actively exploited zero-days—so you should ensure your device stays protected for as long as possible.

        Buying a six-year-old refurbished MacBook in 2026 obviously isn't the right choice for some, but for this sale price of $279.99 at StackSocial, it can make sense for a student, casual home user, or anyone who needs an inexpensive secondary Mac for browsing, documents, email, streaming, and video calls. This is the Intel version rather than the better-known M1 model from later in 2020, so expectations should remain reasonable. It uses a 10th-generation Intel Core i3 processor with 8GB of RAM and Intel Iris Plus graphics, which is fine for writing in Google Docs, keeping a handful of browser tabs open, joining video calls, or watching Netflix, but it's not something I would buy for video editing, modern games, or heavier creative work.Still, the hardware has the sharp 13.3-inch Retina display, the Magic Keyboard is comfortable to type on, and Touch ID makes logging in and approving purchases easier. You also get two Thunderbolt 3 ports, USB-C charging, and a 720p webcam. Apple originally rated this model for up to 11 hours of wireless web use, although a refurbished battery that is six years old may not come close to that figure. StackSocial lists this particular machine as Grade B, so light to moderate scuffs are possible, and the included warranty lasts 30 days.

The bigger concern is how long it will stay useful. This MacBook Air can run macOS Sequoia, but it doesn't support macOS Tahoe 26, so it's already missing out on Apple’s latest major operating system update. That doesn't make it unusable, but it does limit how much life you should expect from it going forward. At $279.99, I would consider it a short-term option for a student, someone who needs a secondary laptop, or a casual user who mostly browses the web, streams video, and works with documents. It makes much less sense for anyone who wants a MacBook to keep for several more years, especially when newer Apple silicon models offer better performance and longer software support.

After each cleaning run, the dock can empty the dustbin, wash the mop pads, dry them, dispense detergent, and keep the robot supplied with clean water. That said, Woot lists it as an Open-Box deal—meaning while the packaging was previously opened (maybe for display or testing), the unit itself is new. title: 10 Hacks Every Audible User Should Know

body:
We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
        
        Audible is one of the largest and most popular audiobook services out there, and with good reason, as it gives you access to a huge library at a competitive price. Unlike Libby—which is also an excellent audiobook platform—you don't have to sit on a wait list for popular titles, and purchases are (mostly) yours to keep. These are the tricks you need to know to get the most out of Audible and save some money along the way. Add narration to Kindle to get audiobooks for free or at a low costIf you like to have the option to either read or listen to your books, you can take advantage of Kindle and Audible crossovers to get the audio version of certain titles for free, or at least less than what you'd pay if you bought them outright on Audible. One option is to add audio upgrades to your purchased Kindle books: you can see which books are eligible and how much the narration add-ons cost using the Matchmaker tool. If you have a Kindle Unlimited subscription, you can also get lots of Prime Reading books with Audible Narration at no additional cost. Finally, when adding a Kindle book to your cart, look for the Add audiobook checkbox to see how much the companion Audible version costs—in some cases, it may be cheaper to purchase the bundle than to use an Audible credit or buy them separately.
Pause your membership instead of canceling to avoid losing creditsFor users on Audible's monthly subscription plans, credits are use it or lose it—if you cancel, your unused credits expire even though you've already paid for them. If you fall behind on your listening or forgot that you've been paying for Audible and want to catch up, you can temporarily pause your membership instead of canceling. This way, you retain your credits without being charged the ongoing fee. You can pause your membership for up to 90 days every 12 months. In the app, go to Profile > Membership > Manage > Pause Membership. 
Use retention offers to get a free credit or discounted subscriptionIf you threaten to cancel your Audible subscription, Amazon may try to keep you by giving you a discount on your membership or applying a free credit to your account. This one isn't a guarantee, but users report that the cancellation flow frequently includes retention offers. There's no harm in trying, and you don't have to confirm the cancellation if there's no incentive. On the Audible web interface, tap your name > Membership Details > Cancel membership. Note that if your subscription is billed through Apple or Google, you have to cancel through the App Store or Google Play Store and may not receive a retention offer. Opt for an annual plan to get credits up front With Audible's standard monthly billing plan—priced at $8.99—you get a credit added to your account each month and listening access for as long as you maintain your membership. If you cancel, you lose unused credits and your existing library. A premium subscription billed monthly at $14.95 lets you keep books purchased with credits even if you cancel, though unused credits will expire immediately. But if you sign up for an annual subscription, you get 12 credits up front, meaning you don't have to wait for your plan to renew to add books to your library, and you don't lose unused credits if you cancel. This plan is also about $2.50 cheaper per credit than a monthly premium subscription, and you get access to additional sales and discounts. If you try to share a single Audible account with multiple users, you won't be able to listen to the same book at the same time without disrupting each other's progress. But you can share purchased titles with other members of your Amazon Family account, which allows keeps individual progress and listening histories separate. An Amazon Family can include two adults and up to four children. Note that you can't share unused credits—only purchased books. Customize your skip times to shorten replay intervals The default skip forward and back times in Audible are 30 seconds, but you can customize these intervals to as little as 10 seconds and as long as 90 seconds. If you frequently find yourself rewinding, especially when listening to dense material, you may want to shorten the interval so you don't have to go back and listen to a longer segment each time you need to repeat a sentence. Note that back and forward can be set at different lengths. Go to Profile > Settings > Player > App display > Back 30s Forward 30s to change the skip times. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use the Clip tool to save and annotate specific audio snippetsAudible's Clip feature saves short segments from your books to reference later. You can also add notes to clips so you don't have to keep a separate document or write down start/end times for snippets. Tap +Clip on the title's player screen to automatically save a 30-second segment, then click Edit on the confirmation banner and use the sliders to mark the exact beginning and end points and enter notes. To play a saved audio clip, open the title's player screen, tap the Clips & Notes button, and identify the clip you want to listen to. You can either play just the clip or start listening again from the clip.  Add items to your wish list to track deals and discountsIf you're waiting for audiobooks to go on sale before you buy them, add titles to your wish list to see deals and discounts at a glance all in one place. You can use the list to regularly check for price updates, and Audible may also send email or push notifications when titles you've saved are on sale. In the Audible app, tap Add to Wish List on the title's detail page, and then view your list via Library > Lists > Wish List. Return purchased titles if you don’t like the book or narrator Audible has a fairly generous return policy, so if you don't like a book or a narrator, you can get your credit back to use on a different title. You must be a Premium subscriber to take advantage of returns, and only audiobooks bought with credits (versus cash) are eligible within 365 days of purchase. Note that you may lose this privilege if you abuse it, so you probably shouldn't listen to every title all the way through and then try to return it. Also, always listen to the book sample if available to make sure you don't hate the narrator. Use Libation or OpenAudible to download and back up your booksIf you purchase titles on Audible, you'd expect that the files are yours to keep—just like a physical book—but this isn't a guarantee. Third-party platforms like Libation and OpenAudible allow you to download, back up, and convert your audiobook files so you can store and listen to them locally. Libation is free and open source but some users note that it's a bit more technical. OpenAudible has some free functionality, but you'll have to buy either an annual or lifetime subscription to get access to file conversion and other premium features.

title: How to Claim Your Piece of Apple's $250 Million Siri Settlement
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 21, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Jakub Porzycki/NurPhoto via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple agreed to settle a lawsuit over delays with Siri AI for $250 million.
                                            If you bought an iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 device between June 10, 2024 and March 29, 2025, you may be eligible for a share.
                                            If you're an eligible claimant, it's now time to submit your claim.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Last week, Apple released Siri AI, the company's biggest overhaul to its smart assistant ever. If you have a compatible device running the latest updates, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate, you now have access to Apple's AI-powered Siri, in addition to a number of new Apple Intelligence features. For some of us, this might seem like a welcome upgrade from a company that hasn't done as much with AI as its competitors. For others, it's a long overdue fulfillment of a promise. So overdue, in fact, that Apple may be offering a payout to make up for it.Delays in launching Siri AI triggered a lawsuitThis year's iOS updates aren't the first we've seen of Siri AI. Back in 2024, Apple advertised a new AI-powered Siri that could understand content on your screen and pull data from your various apps to inform its answers. In Apple's pre-recorded demos, for example, Siri could dive through your texts and emails to locate a family member's travel information if you asked the assistant what time that person's flight arrived. Apple said this new Siri would arrive with iOS 18 later that year, launching on compatible iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 16 devices. But while the company slowly rolled out Apple Intelligence features through the iOS 18 lifecycle, this new Siri was nowhere to be found.For many, this absence ranged from mildly humorous to frustrating. Some, however, found it deceptive. After all, Apple said users who bought a certain iPhone could expect it to run this supercharged Siri. You might have picked up an iPhone 16, or perhaps the previous-generation iPhone 15 Pro, assuming you could take advantage of Apple's AI-powered assistant, but those changes didn't actually arrive until last week, more than two years after Apple first announced them. Depending on your upgrade cycle, you could be on your second or third smartphone since then. 
These grievances weren't confined to grousing on the internet. The Clarkson law firm filed a suit against Apple, alleging the company misled customers with these new Siri features. While the company has not admitted wrongdoing, it did agree to a $250 million settlement to put the case aside. And if you're eligible, it is now time to claim your share of the settlement. Not all iPhone owners are eligible for a slice of this settlement. Per the terms, only customers who bought an iPhone 15, iPhone 15 Pro Max, or any iPhone 16 model (iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, iPhone 16 Pro Max, iPhone 16e) can claim a share. What's more, there's a specific timeline during which purchases are eligible: June 10, 2024, to March 29, 2025. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
If you bought your iPhone 15 Pro or iPhone 16 between these dates, you can make a claim. To start, head to the settlement's official website, then choose "File A Claim." If you have a Claim ID and PIN, you can share them here. If you don't, you can still choose to file a claim online. You can share your iPhone's serial number, though if you don't have it, you can share your Apple Account email address and the number associated with your iPhone. Claims are open from today, Sept. 21, through Dec. 21. How much will you get in the Siri settlement?While $250 million sounds like a huge payout, the final amount likely won't be: The estimated payout is $25 per claimant, though that may change depending on the number of respondents. If there are fewer claims than expected, you may receive as much as $95. As MacRumors reports, the final approval hearing is on Feb. 24 of next year, so don't expect the money any time soon.
